description: Places where Wolff answers the question of a section and Vattel answers it differently (method log, divergence layer). relation: diverges or partly. severity: 3 incompatible answers, 2 different ground or a condition that changes cases, 1 a qualification. Machine judgements, not checked by hand.

items.question: Does a nation's duty to others yield to its duty to itself, and when does it cease?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 206 holds that when a nation's duty to itself collides with its duty to another nation, the duty to itself prevails. Vattel holds that the duty to another ceases only when the nation could not help without essential harm to itself, and counts as possible only what is just and honest. Vattel sets a threshold of essential harm where Wolff lets any collision decide for the duty to self.
items.passage: Lors donc qu'elle ne pour-roit contribuer au bien d'une autre, sans se nuire essentiellement à soi - même , son obligation cesse dans cette occasion particuliere
items.sourcePassage: si officium Gentis erga seipsam colliditur cum officio erga Gentem aliam, officium Gentis erga seipsam vincit

items.question: Are nations masters of their own actions where others' perfect rights are not affected, and may others command them?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1090 gives the whole of nations a universal imperium over each nation, with the right to determine its actions for the common good and to compel it to satisfy its obligation. Vattel holds that a nation bound only by internal obligation is master of its actions, and that others must tolerate its abuse of liberty because they have no right to command it. Vattel denies the power of command that Wolff derives from the civitas maxima.
items.passage: Si elle abuse de sa liberté , elle peche ; mais les autres doivent le souffrir , n'ayant aucun droit de lui commander.
items.sourcePassage: nimirum determinandi actiones singularum salutis communis obtinendae causa et cogendi singulas, ut obligationi suae satisfaciant

items.question: What is the foundation of the voluntary law of nations?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1090 derives the voluntary law of nations from the civitas maxima, a society of nations to which nature supplies both the consent and the laws. Vattel grounds the same body of rules in the liberty, independence and equality of nations, each judging its own duties in conscience, with consent presumed. Vattel states that he departs from Wolff on the foundation of this law while keeping its name.
items.passage: Les nations étant libres , indépendantes , égales , et chacune devant juger en sa conscience de ce qu'elle a à faire pour remplir ses devoirs , l'effet de tout cela est d'opérer , au moins extérieurement et parmi les hommes , une parfaite égalité de droits entre les nations
items.sourcePassage: Atque hoc jus, quod ex notione civitatis maximae derivatur, cum Grotio dicimus Jus Gentium voluntarium

items.question: What is the extent and limit of the general right of nations over the conduct of each sovereign state?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1090 gives the whole of nations a general right to determine the actions of each nation for the common good and to compel it. Vattel holds that nations together have no right over the conduct of each except insofar as their natural society is concerned, and measures that right by the end of the society. Vattel keeps a right to repress violators of the law of nations but drops the general power to direct each nation's conduct.
items.passage: toutes ensemble n'ont donc aucun droit sur la conduite de chacune , sinon entant que la société naturelle s'y trouve intéressée
items.sourcePassage: nimirum determinandi actiones singularum salutis communis obtinendae causa et cogendi singulas, ut obligationi suae satisfaciant

items.question: Does a nation have a right to whatever is necessary for its preservation?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 32 holds that every nation has a right to whatever it cannot preserve itself without. Vattel holds the same right but excludes means that are unjust in themselves, and declares the obligation void in a case where no other means exist. The added exclusion limits the right to means that natural law does not absolutely forbid.
items.passage: on comprend bien sans doute, que ces moyens ne doivent pas être injustes en eux - mêmes et de ceux que la loi naturelle proscrit absolument.
items.sourcePassage: Genti unicuique competit jus ad ea , sine quibus se conservare nequit.

items.question: Does a nation have a right to whatever is necessary for its preservation?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 46 holds that a law of nature obliging to an end gives a right to the means, and that the same right covers the means when only one exists. Vattel holds that when the only available means is one natural law forbids, the obligation is impossible and void in that case. Vattel resolves the single-means case by cancelling the obligation where Wolff's rule extends the right to whatever single means remains.
items.passage: si en quelque occasion particuliere, il ne s'en présente point d'autres pour satisfaire à une obligation générale, l'obligation doit passer, dans ce cas particulier, pour impossible , et nulle par conséquent.
items.sourcePassage: Quodsi ergo lex naturae obligat ad finem, jus quoque dat ad media, consequenter si medium nonnisi unicum fuerit, jure eodem utimur.

items.question: In what sense does the sovereign represent the nation?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 39 holds that once the nation transfers its rights, the moral person that subsisted in the whole nation now subsists in the ruler, and nothing of its dignity remains in the people. Vattel holds that the moral person acts only in and through the sovereign without wholly ceasing to exist in the nation. Vattel keeps a residual personality in the nation that Wolff's transfer leaves nowhere but in the ruler.
items.passage: c'est en lui que se trouve la personne morale , qui , sans cesser absolument d'exister dans la nation , n'agit désormais qu'en lui et par lui
items.sourcePassage: persona ista moralis, quae antea in Gente universa subsistebat, nunc in alio individuo physico subsistit

items.question: In what sense is the prince subject to the laws
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 984 holds that laws an absolute ruler sets for himself are not fundamental laws, so he is not always bound to observe them and may abolish them entirely if he sees fit. Vattel also places the absolute prince above the laws, but lets him dispense himself only when natural justice and equity permit. Vattel further binds the prince in his private affairs to the laws of property and to certain laws of general police.
items.passage: il peut s'en dispenser lui - même , toutes les fois que la justice et l'équité naturelles le lui permettent
items.sourcePassage: Rector civitatis non semper necessario easdem observare tenetur, immo si ita visum fuerit, eas prorsus tollere potest

items.question: What are so-called patrimonial states / can a state be a patrimony
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 982 defends the patrimonial kingdom, in which the ruler holds sovereignty by right of property and may dispose of it as he sees fit. Vattel rejects the expression and holds that a state cannot be a patrimony. What Wolff calls a patrimonial kingdom becomes for Vattel a power to name a successor that the nation has entrusted to its prince.
items.passage: Nous avons fait voir ( §. 61. ) que l'état ne peut être un patrimoine.
items.sourcePassage: Quodsi enim regnum sit patrimoniale, imperium jure proprietatis possidet

items.question: Obligation to cultivate external commerce and its ground
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 211 grounds each nation's obligation to promote commerce among nations in the common good of the civitas maxima and the welfare of all nations. Vattel grounds the obligation to cultivate foreign commerce in the good of the state itself and the needs of its citizens. The rule is the same, but the ground moves from the society of nations to the nation's duty to itself.
items.passage: Par la même raison tirée du bien de l'état , et aussi pour procurer aux citoyens toutes les choses dont ils ont besoin , une nation est obligée d'exercer et de favoriser le commerce extérieur.
items.sourcePassage: Gentes enim commercia invicem exercere naturaliter obligantur, quantum in potestate est ( §. 187. ) et, quatenus in civitatem maximam coivisse intelliguntur, commune bonum promovere ( §. 12. )

items.question: Does a mere permission to trade give a perfect right, and may a nation withdraw or restrict it (and refuse trade altogether)?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 75 holds that the natural duty to trade does not remove a nation's freedom to decide about commerce at its discretion, and he approves the Chinese refusal of foreign trade. Vattel accepts the freedom to withdraw a mere permission, but allows a nation to refuse trade altogether only when its duties to itself require this for serious and important reasons. Without such reasons Vattel holds the nation bound by the general duties of humanity.
items.passage: il faut que ses devoirs envers elle - même lui prescrivent cette réserve , par des raisons sérieuses et importantes ; autrement elle ne peut se refuser aux devoirs généraux de l'humanité
items.sourcePassage: non tamen hinc sequitur, naturaliter ita obligari Gentes ad commercia cum aliis exercenda, ut libertas de iis pro arbitrio statuendi tollatur

items.question: Are commercial rights founded on a treaty lost by long non-use?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 78 holds that rights of mere faculty are lost only once a prohibition or coercion has been obeyed with sufficient sign of consent. Vattel applies the same rule to commercial rights acquired by treaty but adds that such a right is lost when the holder fails a tacit condition of the grant. His example is a nation that granted the right in order to secure a supply it needed and may give an exclusive privilege to another supplier.
items.passage: la nation qui avoit ce droit de vendre le perdra ainsi , parce qu'elle n'en a pas rempli la condition tacite
items.sourcePassage: jus merae facultatis praescribitur, ex quo tempore intercesserit prohibitio, aut coactio, eique paritum est cum sufficienti consensus significatione

items.question: What does 'patrie' mean (and can it change)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 140 defines patria as the land or city where one's parents were domiciled at one's birth, and he ties the rights of the law of nations to that sense. Vattel holds that in the law of nations patrie means the state of which one is a member at present. For Vattel the birth sense is a narrower one, and the duties owed to the patrie attach to the state one has joined.
items.passage: Il signifiecommunément l'état dont on est membre : c'est en ce sens que nous l'avons employé dans les paragraphes précédens , et qu'il doit être pris dans le droit des gens.
items.sourcePassage: Patria dicitur locus, nimirum terra, vel urbs, in qua parentes, dum quis nascitur, domicilium habent

items.question: What constitutes a nation's power
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 69 places a nation's power in the number of men able to bear arms and in its wealth, and counts hired foreign soldiers as part of that power. Vattel places the power of a state in three things: the number of citizens, their military virtues and wealth. Vattel adds the military virtue of the citizens as a distinct component of power.
items.passage: La puissance d'un état consiste en trois choses, le nombre des citoyens , leurs vertus militaires, et les richesses.
items.sourcePassage: potentia Gentis consistit in multitudine hominum, qui militiae munera exercere valent, et in divitiis ejusdem

items.question: Remedy of the protected nation when the protector claims more right than the treaty gives
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 83 allows the protected nation, when the protector claims more right than the pact gives, to resist by force and to implore foreign aid. Vattel holds that the protected nation may regard the treaty as broken and provide for its own safety as it judges best. Vattel reports Wolff's narrower remedy as the opinion of some writers and treats the breach as dissolving the treaty itself.
items.passage: celle-ci peut regarder le traité comme rompu , et pourvoir à sa sûreté suivant sa prudence.
items.sourcePassage: vi resistere et auxilium alienum implorare licet.

items.question: Whether the protected nation's silence in the face of encroachment creates a right for the usurper
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 84 holds that the long silence of the protected nation is presumed to be abandonment of its right and consent to the usurpation, so that the protector acquires the usurped right and even supreme power. Vattel accepts that long silence forms a tacit consent but requires the silence to be voluntary. A nation that proves its opposition was stifled by violence or fear loses nothing by its silence.
items.passage: Mais il faut bien observer que le silence , pour marquer un consentement tacite , doit être volontaire.
items.sourcePassage: ex diuturno silentio jus suum derelinquere et in usurpationem ejus consentire praesumitur

items.question: Who are citizens and natives, and do children follow their fathers' condition?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 140 holds that the rights attached to one's patria are constituted by human will and are purely positive, not natural, so that a nation may grant none. Vattel holds that the children of citizens follow their fathers' condition naturally, because the society can only maintain and perpetuate itself through them. The rights of birth rest for Wolff on positive law and for Vattel on the society's duty of self-preservation and the citizens' presumed reservation.
items.passage: La société ne pouvant se soutenir et se perpétuer que par les enfans des citoyens , ces enfans y suivent naturellement la condition de leurs peres , et entrent dans tous leurs droits.
items.sourcePassage: Jura autem ista cum voluntate hominum constituantur, etsi principiis Juris naturalis convenienter, naturalia non sunt, sed mere positiva

items.question: Who may grant naturalisation, and is the sovereign's power to do so limited?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 134 makes naturalisation depend on the will of the people and hence of the ruler who holds or exercises the people's right. Vattel holds that the fundamental law may limit the prince to an imperfect naturalisation or require the concurrence of the nation's deputies. Vattel also records that in England birth in the country alone naturalises the children of a foreigner.
items.passage: C'est une disposition de la loi fondamentale, qui limite le pouvoir du prince.
items.sourcePassage: Facile autem patet, a voluntate populi dependere, consequenter Rectoris civitatis, qui populi jus habet, seu exercet (§. 34. 42. part. 8. Jur. nat.), utrum jurium illorum, quae ab indigenatu pendent, participem facere velit advenam, vel peregrinum, nec ne.

items.question: May a person leave his native country or society?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1019 forbids leaving the state without the express or tacit consent of the superior, who judges whether the state can spare the subject and need not permit the rich or the useful to depart. Vattel holds that every man has the right to leave his country to settle elsewhere when this does not compromise its good. The superior's consent is a condition of lawful departure for Wolff and no condition at all for Vattel, who leaves only a duty of honour against leaving without need.
items.passage: Tout homme a le droit de quitter son pays, pour s'établir ailleurs, quand par cette démarche il ne compromet point le bien de sa patrie.
items.sourcePassage: sine consensu superioris sive expresso, sive tacito a civitate discedere non licet.

items.question: In what cases is a citizen entitled to leave his country?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 153 defines the right of emigration as a permission of voluntary exile, granted to subjects who adhere to a religion the ruler will not tolerate. Vattel holds that such dissenters have an absolute right to withdraw with their goods and families, grounded in the limits of the social pact. Wolff grounds emigration in the ruler's permission, and Vattel in a right against the ruler that places the breach of the pact on the intolerant.
items.passage: ceux qui croyent et professent une autre religion sont en droit de se retirer, d'emporter leurs biens et d'emmener leurs familles.
items.sourcePassage: Ita jus emigrandi competit subditis, quibus e civitate discedere permittitur, quia religioni, quam Rector civitatis tolerare non vult, addicti sunt.

items.question: In what cases is a citizen entitled to leave his country?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 154 holds that the right of emigration arises only from a pact, a fundamental law or the will of the superior. Vattel holds that in certain cases a citizen is absolutely entitled to leave his country by reasons drawn from the social pact itself, as when he cannot find subsistence, when the society fails its obligations to him, or when laws are imposed on matters of conscience. For Wolff the right depends on a positive grant; for Vattel it binds the sovereign without any grant.
items.passage: Il est des cas dans lesquels un citoyen est absolument en droit, par des raisons prises du pacte même de la société politique, de renoncer à sa patrie et de l'abandonner.
items.sourcePassage: jus emigrandi nascitur vel ex pacto, aut lege fundamentali, vel a voluntate superioris dependet.

items.question: What are the sources of the citizens' right of emigration?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 154 derives the right of emigration from three sources only: a pact with other nations, a fundamental law, or the ruler's permission. Vattel accepts these three sources and places before them a natural right reserved to citizens in the pact of civil association itself. The added source makes emigration in the cases of § 223 independent of the sovereign's will.
items.passage: c'est un droit naturel, qui leur est certainement réservé dans le pacte même d'association civile
items.sourcePassage: jus emigrandi nascitur vel ex pacto, aut lege fundamentali, vel a voluntate superioris dependet.

items.question: Is there an exception allowing any nation to punish foreign-committed crimes that endanger the safety of mankind?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 151 holds without exception that a person who committed a crime in one nation cannot be punished by another nation to which he comes. Vattel accepts the territorial rule but exempts habitual poisoners, assassins, incendiaries and pirates as enemies of mankind, who may be punished wherever they are seized. The exception rests on an injury to the common safety of all nations, which Wolff's requirement of a direct injury to the punishing nation excludes.
items.passage: Les empoisonneurs, les assassins, les incendiaires de profession peuvent être exterminés partout où on les saisit
items.sourcePassage: Patet itaque, qui apud Gentem unam deliquit, aut crimen aliquod perpetravit, puniri non posse ab alia Gente, ad quam is venit.

items.question: Can the nation cede use and ownership of common goods to the ruler, and how?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 99 holds that the people may transfer dominion of public things to the ruler, with the use wholly or at least partly remaining with the people. Vattel holds that the nation may give the ruler the use of common goods alone, and even their property, but only by an express act. Vattel allows the use itself to pass to the ruler and excludes a transfer by tacit consent.
items.passage: Mais ce transport d'usage ou de propriété exige un acte exprès du propriétaire, qui est la nation.
items.sourcePassage: populus quoque rerum publicarum dominium in Rectorem civitatis transferre potest (§. 12. part. 3. Jur. nat.), usu tamen vel omni, vel saltem aliquo manente penes populum

items.question: Whether the prince may dismember the state without the nation's consent
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 1007 holds that a patrimonial king may alienate the whole realm or part of it by a peace treaty without the people's consent, while a usufructuary king needs that consent. Vattel makes the answer depend on the fundamental law: where it forbids dismemberment the prince needs the nation's concurrence, and where it is silent the prince with absolute power acts only as depositary of the nation's rights and may cede only from necessity. Vattel drops the patrimonial kingdom as a ground for alienation without consent.
items.passage: Si la loi fondamentale défend au souverain tout démembrement, il ne peut le faire sans le concours de la nation , ou de ses représentans.
items.sourcePassage: Si per pacem vel imperium totum, vel pars ejus alienari debet, et regnum fuerit patrimoniale, Rex id facere potest, sine populi consensu

items.question: Who owns a river separating two territories
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 106 assigns a boundary river to the nation that occupied it first, divides it at the middle when occupation was simultaneous or doubtful, and otherwise defers to treaties. Vattel keeps these rules but presumes that the first settler on one bank occupied the adjoining river, more strongly the narrower the river, and adds long uncontested possession as a title. Immemorial possession can give one nation the whole river where Wolff's presumption would divide it.
items.passage: Une longue possession, non-contredite , établit le droit des nations
items.sourcePassage: dominium et imperium in flumine erit ejus Gentis, quae prior id occupavit

items.question: What happens to the bed and the river when a boundary river wholly changes course
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 246 holds that when a river wholly abandons its natural bed, the bed remains with the owner of the river. Vattel holds that when a public river changes course within a state, the abandoned bed accrues by halves to the adjoining arcifinious lands through their right of alluvion. The public keeps the bed only where the adjacent lands are not arcifinious.
items.passage: Le lit abandonné accroît par moitié aux terres contigues de part et d'autre , si elles sont arcisinies
items.sourcePassage: eum manere ejus, cujus est flumen

items.question: May a nation appropriate the use of the open sea
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 121 holds that no nation may subject the open sea to its dominion because its use is inexhaustible, and he states the rule without exception. Vattel reaches the same conclusion but adds that a nation may subject a thing of inexhaustible use to its domination if its free and common use is harmful or dangerous to that nation's security. He denies only that this exception applies to the open sea.
items.passage: Si le libre et commun usage d'une chose de cette nature étoit nuisible ou dangereux à une nation , le soin de sa propre sûreté l'autoriseroit à soumettre , si elle le pouvoit, cette chose-là à sa domination, afin de n'en permettre l'usage qu'avec les précautions que lui dicteroit la prudence.
items.sourcePassage: nulli quoque Genti vastum mare, etsi fieri posset, dominio suo subjicere licet, nec salvo jure naturali dominium ejus acquirere valet

items.question: Does such exclusion wrong all nations, entitling them to unite against it
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 125 holds that a nation which excludes others from the open sea by arms wrongs all nations, and that all are naturally obliged to resist it because nations are understood to have united in a civitas maxima. Vattel holds that all nations may and must unite against such a nation, but he grounds the duty in their common interest in the law of nations and in their duties to themselves and to human society. The obligation is the same; the civitas maxima is dropped as its ground.
items.passage: elles s'acquitteront de leurs devoirs envers elles-mêmes et envers la société humaine dont elles sont membres
items.sourcePassage: immo quatenus Gentes in civitatem maximam coivisse intelliguntur (§. 10.), ad idem tuendum naturaliter obligantur (§. 12.)

items.question: Can the sea near the coasts be appropriated by the coastal nation?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 128 holds that coastal nations may occupy the adjacent sea, including its fisheries, as far as they can defend their dominion there. Vattel accepts the appropriation of coastal fisheries but adds that a nation which has once recognised the common right of other peoples to fish there can no longer exclude them. Prior acknowledgement of common use thus extinguishes a right of appropriation that Wolff leaves open.
items.passage: Mais si, loin de s'en emparer, il a une fois reconnu le droit commun des autres peuples d'y venir pêcher , il ne peut plus les en exclure
items.sourcePassage: Partes maris a Gentibus, quae idem accolunt, occupari possunt, quousque dominium in iisdem tueri possunt.

items.question: How far may a nation's dominion over the adjacent sea extend?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 128 measures a nation's dominion over the adjacent sea by how far it can defend that dominion, and he rejects Grotius's further restriction as arbitrary. Vattel measures it by two conditions: the extent necessary for the state's security and the extent it can make respected. The added test of necessity for a legitimate end limits a claim that defensive capacity alone would allow.
items.passage: en général la domination de l'état sur la mer voisine va aussi loin qu'il est nécessaire pour sa sûreté, et qu'il peut la faire respecter
items.sourcePassage: quousque dominium in iisdem tueri possunt

items.question: Does occupying parts of the sea give the nation empire/jurisdiction over them?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 129 holds that a nation which occupies part of the sea acquires empire together with domain, and he derives the right to exclude others from domain alone. Vattel accepts this but adds that empire and domain are separable, so that a nation may hold empire over a stretch of sea without any property in it. Empire is presumed from domain, but domain is not presumed from empire.
items.passage: Il est vrai cependant que l'empire et le domaine , ou la propriété ne sont pas inséparables de la nature, même pour un état souverain
items.sourcePassage: si qua Gens partem quandam maris occupat, cum dominio imperium in iis simul occupat

items.question: May a nation acquire a commercial monopoly by treaty, and what if it abuses it by excessive prices?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 210 holds that a nation which sells goods obtainable nowhere else at an unfair price sins but does no injury to the buying nations, and he distinguishes impunity from right. Vattel agrees for conveniences, but holds that where the goods are necessities and the price excessive, other nations are authorised to unite and coerce the monopolist. Vattel grounds this exception in self-preservation and the good of human society, not in an injury done.
items.passage: Mais s'il étoit question de choses nécessaires à la vie, et que le monopoleur voulut les porter à un prix excessif, les autres nations seroient autorisées par le soin de leur propre salut, et pour l'avantage de la société humaine, à se réunir pour mettre à la raison un avide oppresseur.
items.sourcePassage: in hypothesi propositionis praesentis Genti ementi injuria nulla fit

items.question: May a nation acquire a commercial monopoly by treaty, and what if it abuses it by excessive prices?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1112 holds that a nation may secure a trade monopoly by treaty and commits no injury if it sells the goods at an unfair price, since the owner may abuse his right. Vattel accepts the monopoly and the absence of injury under external right, but adds that where necessities of life are priced excessively, other nations may combine to force the monopolist to reason. The distinction between necessities and mere conveniences opens a case for coercion that Wolff's rule excludes.
items.passage: les autres nations seroient autorisées par le soin de leur propre salut, et pour l'avantage de la société humaine, à se réunir pour mettre à la raison un avide oppresseur
items.sourcePassage: nulla committitur injuria, si pretio parum aequo vendantur

items.question: Can a nation claim precedence by right, and how is priority of rank settled?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 238 derives from the natural equality of nations that no nation may arrogate any right that other nations lack. Vattel agrees that no nation has a right to precedence, but holds it reasonable that a small state cede first place to a powerful one, and gives weight to the antiquity of a state. Power and age become grounds for a ceremonial order of rank that Wolff's argument from equality does not provide.
items.passage: il est raisonnable que celui-ci lui cede, dans les occasions où il faut que l'un cede à l'autre
items.sourcePassage: Gens quoque nulla naturaliter jus quoddam sibi arrogare potest, quod aliis Gentibus non competit

items.question: Must other nations give a ruler the title his people give him?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 246 holds that whether other nations give a ruler the name and titles his subjects give him depends solely on their will, and that they are bound only by request or pact. Vattel holds that giving a ruler the title his people give him, when it is reasonable by received usage, belongs to the natural duties binding nations, and that distant nations may not refuse a royal title the ruler's neighbours already accord. Vattel grounds the practice in duty and established usage where Wolff leaves it to free consent.
items.passage: il est tout à fait convenableaux devoirs naturels qui lient les nations, de donner à un souverain, ou au conducteur quelconque d'un état, le même titre que lui donne son peuple
items.sourcePassage: Quamobrem patet, an Gentes aliae hoc facere velint, ab ipsarum unice voluntate dependere.

items.question: How much circumspection is required in religious proselytism?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 261 holds that a nation is naturally obliged to contribute whatever it can, including missionaries and books, to persuade other nations of the true worship of God, desisting only in doubtful cases. Vattel holds that zeal for proselytism endangers the peace of nations, since every people believes its own religion true, and that preaching abroad should await an invitation from foreign peoples or a certain divine mission. Wolff's duty of humanity to propagate true religion becomes in Vattel a restraint on unsolicited missions.
items.passage: en attendant les dispositions de la providence, une invitation des peuples étrangers, ou une mission divine bien certaine, pour la prêcher au dehors, il trouve assez d'occupation dans la patrie
items.sourcePassage: Quicquid Gens una ad persuadendum aliis verum Dei cultum conferre potest; ad id conferendum naturaliter obligatur.

items.question: May a sovereign act on behalf of co-religionists persecuted in another state?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 258 holds that when a ruler overburdens or treats his subjects too harshly, another ruler may not resist him by force and may only intercede. Vattel restricts foreign nations to intercession for persecuted co-religionists unless persecution reaches intolerable excess, which counts as manifest tyranny and permits aid to the oppressed, and he adds the security of the intervening states as a further ground. The exception for extreme oppression licenses the forcible intervention that Wolff excludes.
items.passage: mais c'est là tout ce qu'elles peuvent faire légitimement, à moins que la persécution ne soit portée jusqu'à des excès intolérables
items.sourcePassage: Rector alterius civitatis vi resistere nequit; pro iis tamen intercedere potest.

items.question: What does jurisdiction include, and when may a prince intervene for subjects abroad in a foreign judgment?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 587 holds that between nations a judge's sentence, well or badly given, is not held true and just even when confirmed on appeal, so that a sentence plainly against right in an undoubted matter counts as denial of justice. Vattel holds that a final sentence regularly pronounced must be held just and executed as such, and that examining its justice attacks the jurisdiction of the sovereign who gave it. Vattel admits intervention only for denial of justice, evident injustice, manifest breach of forms or odious discrimination, so that the presumption Wolff denies between nations becomes the rule.
items.passage: toute sentence définitive , prononcée régulierement , soit tenue pour juste et exécutée comme telle
items.sourcePassage: inter Gentes sententia judicis seu bene, seu male prolata pro vera et justa non habetur, etiamsi a superiore fuerit confirmata

items.question: Who owns deserted and uncultivated places inside a nation's territory?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 275 holds that deserted, barren and uncultivated places within a nation's region belong to the nation, and that only the nation or its ruler may dispose of them. Vattel holds the same but adds that no nation may legitimately appropriate a disproportionate extent of land and so leave other peoples without dwelling and subsistence. Vattel makes a nation's title to unused land depend on its having a reason to retain it, as with the Roman frontier strip along the Rhine.
items.passage: Aucune nation ne peut légitimement s'approprier une étendue de pays trop disproportionnée , et réduire ainsi les autres peuples à manquer de demeure et de subsistance.
items.sourcePassage: ea Gentis sunt, consequenter de iis disponere nequit nisi Gens, aut Rector civitatis

items.question: May the sovereign forbid entry into his territory, and on what terms?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 296 holds that the lord of a territory may forbid foreigners to enter under a penalty, provided the prohibition and penalty are made known, and he cites the Chinese capital penalty as an instance. Vattel accepts the right of prohibition but holds the Chinese ban just only on condition that the aid of humanity was not refused to those driven to the frontier by storm or necessity. Vattel adds a necessity exception that Wolff's rule does not contain.
items.passage: pourvu que l'on ne refusât point les secours de l'humanité à ceux que la tempête , ou quelque nécessité contraignoit de se présenter à la frontiere
items.sourcePassage: si dominus territorii prohibet, ne quis peregrinus territorium ingrediatur , poenam in ingredientem decernere, seu sub certa poena id prohibere potest

items.question: What if several nations simultaneously occupy the same vacant land?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 308 holds that nations occupying vacant land at the same time each acquire dominion and empire in the part they occupied, and that a division by agreement is merely more advisable, since neither can be compelled to it. Vattel holds that such nations ought to agree and make an equitable division, and that each keeps the portions where it first settled only if they cannot agree. Vattel turns Wolff's counsel of prudence into a duty, while the result in default of agreement is the same.
items.passage: elles doivent convenir entr'elles , et faire un partage équitable
items.sourcePassage: consultius tamen est, ut de divisione inter se conveniant

items.question: Who owns land held by independent families (settled or wandering) and may anyone take empire over them?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1126 holds that the lands serving the use of wandering families are in mixed communion and that the rest remains in primitive communion, open to occupation. Vattel holds that pastoral peoples possess their country exclusively and that no other nation may confine them to a smaller space, even though cultivation would let them live on less, unless it is in absolute want of land. Vattel adds a necessity exception permitting settlement in land already in pastoral use, a case Wolff's division of the land does not provide for.
items.passage: Cependant aucune autre nation n'est en droit de les resserrer , à moins qu'elle ne manquât absolument de terres.
items.sourcePassage: fundi, qui ipsorum usui inservire possunt, in communione mixta sunt (§. 197.), ceteris, utpote non occupatis, in communione primaeva manentibus (§. 210.)

items.question: Are foreigners subject to local laws by tacit condition of entry?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 300 holds that foreigners tacitly promise to subject their actions to the laws of the place, so that those laws have the same force on them as on citizens. Vattel limits the tacit submission to general laws made to maintain good order, excluding laws that relate to the quality of citizen or subject. Wolff makes a comparable reservation for the foreigner's continuing citizenship only later, in Jus gentium § 324.
items.passage: j'entends aux loix générales , faites pour maintenir le bon ordre , et qui ne se rapportent pas à la qualité de citoyen ou de sujet de l'état
items.sourcePassage: eadem vis legum in ipsos est, quae in cives

items.question: Which judge decides foreigners' disputes?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 302 holds that disputes between foreigners, or between a foreigner and a citizen, are to be decided by the judge of the place according to the laws of the place. Vattel repeats this rule but adds that every defendant must be sued before his own judge, the judge of his domicile or of the place where a sudden dispute arises, and that disputes over land go to the state where the land lies. The forum of the defendant and the forum of the situs restrict Wolff's unqualified judge of the place.
items.passage: tout défendeur doit être poursuivi par devant son juge , qui seul a le droit de le condamner et de le contraindre
items.sourcePassage: a judice loci juxta leges loci sunt definiendae

items.question: Which law governs a foreigner's will (form and content)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 326 holds that a foreigner must make his will according to the laws of his domicile and that it cannot otherwise be valid, even where local law does not require those solemnities. Vattel holds that the testator should observe the formalities of the country where he makes the will, unless the law of his own state orders otherwise. On form the two adopt opposite default rules, the law of the domicile for Wolff and the law of the place of execution for Vattel.
items.passage: il paroît que le testateur doit observer celles qui sont établies dans le pays où il teste , à moins que la loi de l'état dont il est membre n'en ordonne autrement
items.sourcePassage: si testamentum condit, id secundum leges in loco domicilii praescriptas facere tenetur, nec aliter validum esse potest

items.question: Is the droit d'aubaine (escheat of foreigners' estates) just
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 330 holds that the droit d'aubaine is contrary to the law of nations and admissible only by way of exception in rare cases of collision between a nation's duties to itself and to others. Vattel holds that natural law tolerates its exercise only by way of retorsion against nations that apply it to one's own subjects. The two agree that the right is unjust but ground the exception differently, in a collision of duties for Wolff and in reciprocity for Vattel.
items.passage: La loi naturelle ne peut en souffrir l'exercice , que par maniere de rétorsion.
items.sourcePassage: jus albinagii admitti non potest nisi per modum exceptionis in casibus particularibus collisionis officiorum Gentium erga seipsas et erga alias

items.question: May a nation in pressing need use foreigners' ships, carts, horses or labour, and on what terms?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 342 holds that a nation threatened by present danger may use the ships, carts, horses and labour of foreigners, even against the owner's will, and states no duty to pay. Vattel grants the same right only where the owners are not in the same necessity, and requires the nation to pay for the use if it is able. The right of necessity becomes in Vattel a paid requisition limited by the owners' own need.
items.passage: elle doit payer l'usage qu'elle en fait , si elle a dequoi le payer
items.sourcePassage: quin praetervehentes cogi possint, ut equorum suorum usum concedant, dubitandum non est

items.question: May a nation short of women take them by force from neighbours, and does this make the abducted women lawful wives?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 341 holds that necessity makes the abduction of virgins lawful for a people of men refused marriage by its neighbours, and cites the Romans as an example. Vattel allows force only to secure the liberty of seeking wives, and denies that any woman may be constrained in her choice or become by right the wife of her ravisher. He also denies the Romans any right if they were a band of brigands rather than a just state.
items.passage: aucune fille en particulier ne peut être contrainte dans son choix, ni devenir de droit la femme d'un ravisseur
items.sourcePassage: necessitatem virginum raptum facere licitum

items.question: May a people driven from home claim a dwelling in a foreign country, and may they stay by force?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 148 holds that reception of an exile depends solely on the will of the people, so that the exile must seek reception and bear a refusal. Vattel holds that a nation must grant a people driven from its home at least temporary habitation unless it has very grave reasons, and that fugitives refused by all may justly settle in the first country with land to spare. Vattel turns the residual right of habitation into a claim enforceable by necessity against the territorial sovereign, subject to bearable conditions.
items.passage: ils pourront avec justice se fixer dans le premier pays où ils trouveront assez de terres, sans en priver les habitans
items.sourcePassage: exul receptum quaerere tenetur, nec prosus pro arbitrio suo domicilium sibi constituere potest, ubi libuerit, et, si receptus denegatur, id ferendum

items.question: What further grounds establish prescription between nations, and does fear-induced silence defeat it?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 363 holds that prescription does not run against one who alleges reasons for his long silence, and that prescription between nations founded on silence alone is almost never of use. Vattel grounds prescription between nations on the peace of peoples and the safety of states, and holds that one who kept silent through fear must bear the loss of his right. Wolff rests prescription on presumed abandonment, which an explanation of silence defeats, while Vattel rests it on the need for stable possession, which such an explanation does not defeat.
items.passage: Si quelqu'un a gardé le silence par crainte, par une espece de nécessité , la perte de son droit est un malheur , qu'il doit souffrir patiemment, puisqu'il n'a pû l'éviter.
items.sourcePassage: Qui silentii diuturni rationes allegat, adversus eum non valet praescriptio.

items.question: Who may make public treaties
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 373 holds that a pact is a treaty only if both parties are supreme powers and its matter concerns the public good. Vattel agrees that sovereigns' private pacts are not public treaties, but admits treaties by princes or communities holding the right by concession of the sovereign, fundamental law, reservation or custom. The German princes and imperial cities and certain subject Swiss towns thereby fall within the law of treaties.
items.passage: n'empêche point que des traités de cette nature ne puissent être faits par des princes, ou des communautés, qui en auront le droit, soit par la concession du souverain , soit par la loi fondamentale de l'état, par des réserves, ou par la coutume
items.sourcePassage: Nimirum ad foedus utrumque requiritur, ut paciscentes sint summae potestates et ut materia, de qua sit pactio, ad bonum publicum pertineat.

items.question: Treaties concluded through plenipotentiaries/mandataries
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 372 holds that those mandated by the supreme power may make treaties, and that their right is defined by the mandate under the ordinary rules of mandate. Vattel applies the same rules but adds that princes now reserve ratification, so that what a plenipotentiary concludes has no force until ratified. He also requires strong reasons, chiefly a departure from instructions, for an honourable refusal to ratify.
items.passage: Tout ce qu'à conclule ministre demeurant sans force jusqu'à la ratification du prince , il y a moins de danger à lui donner un plein pouvoir.
items.sourcePassage: Quantum vero sit jus eorum, quibus hoc negotium mandatur, ex mandato definiendum, cujus fines excedere nequit qui mandatum habet.

items.question: Does an alliance for the defence of the king and royal family survive his deposition, and must the ally defend him?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 422 holds that an alliance for the defence of the king and royal family survives his expulsion, and that the ally must defend him alike against rebellious subjects and against an invader. Vattel holds that the ally must not assist the king against a nation that has formally deposed him for abuse of power, and that doing so injures that nation. Support is owed only in doubtful cases where the nation has not pronounced freely, and never as an endless war.
items.passage: L'allié personnel de ce roi ne doit donc point l'assister contre la nation, qui a usé de son droit en le déposant : s'il l'entreprend, il fait injure à cette nation.
items.sourcePassage: Non minus contra illos, quam hunc foederatus eum recte defendit et, cum foedera sint servanda ( §. 390. b. et §. 789. part. 3. Jur. nat. ), defendere debet.

items.question: Does a real alliance with a state bind the ally when the nation deposes its king or changes its government?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 426 holds that a treaty made by a king is made with the nation and subsists when the king is expelled or deposed, the ally being bound to accept the nation's judgment. Vattel agrees that the ally remains ally of the state and may not judge its domestic changes. He adds that the ally may renounce the alliance if the change of government makes it useless, dangerous or disagreeable.
items.passage: Toutefois si ce changement lui rend l'alliance inutile, dangereuse, ou désagréable, il est le maître d'y renoncer.
items.sourcePassage: Item etiam patet, si Rege expulso, aut deposito fiat liber, vel Regem alium eligat; nisi foedus initum personae ejus defendendae causa ( §. 421. ).

items.question: Does violation of one treaty release the injured ally from other, independent treaties?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 431 holds that breach of one treaty gives the injured ally no right to withdraw from a separate, unbroken treaty, since the obligations of distinct treaties do not depend on one another. Vattel agrees that the breach does not directly release the injured party, but allows him to threaten renunciation of all other treaties and to carry it out if the threat is ignored. Vattel grounds this in the right of the injured party in the state of nature to seize or withhold the offender's rights until satisfaction.
items.passage: Mais l'allié offensé peut menacer celui qui manque à un traité, de renoncer de son côté à tous les autres qui les lient ensemble, et effectuer sa menace, si l'autre n'en tient compte.
items.sourcePassage: Quodsi alterutrum horum foederum servare nolit, aut olim foedus non servavit foederatus; nullum parti alteri jus est recedendi a foedere non violato.

items.question: Does violation of one article release the injured party from the whole treaty?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 432 holds that articles of one treaty on unconnected matters count as distinct treaties, so breach of one article gives no immediate right to withdraw from the whole treaty, only a right to threaten withdrawal. Vattel, citing Wolff, rejects this principle as untenable and holds that all articles of one treaty are reciprocal promises with the force of conditions. Breach of any article therefore entitles the other party to treat the whole treaty as void.
items.passage: Tout ce qui est compris dans un même traité, a donc la force et la nature des promesses réciproques, à moins qu'il n'en soit formellement excepté.
items.sourcePassage: si foederatus unus quoad unam praestationem foedus violat, propterea alteri nondum jus est a toto foedere recedendi

items.question: Does a treaty lapse when one contracting nation is destroyed, and what survives?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 436 holds that every treaty is extinguished when the contracting people perishes, because the agreed performances are personal and become impossible. Vattel holds that treaties requiring reciprocal performance perish with the nation, including by conquest and loss of independence. He exempts conveyances that give an acquired and consummated right, and the nation's debts, which survive the conquest.
items.passage: Mais il ne faut point confondre ici les traités ou les alliances, qui portant l'obligation de prestations réciproques, ne peuvent subsister que par la conservation des puissances contractantes, avec ces contrats qui donnent un droit acquis et consommé, indépendant de toute prestation mutuelle.
items.sourcePassage: Quemadmodum itaque Rege mortuo foedus personale extinguitur ( §. 413. ); ita etiam foedus quodlibet extinguitur populo intereunte.

items.question: What becomes of a nation's existing alliances when it places itself under another's protection?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 439 holds that when one ally places itself under the tutelage of a third nation the alliance subsists unchanged, and neither party may withdraw without the other's consent. Vattel holds that old alliances subsist only so far as they are compatible with the treaty of protection. In a war between the protector and an old ally, the protected state must side with the protector, whose treaty overrides the others.
items.passage: Mais si le cas arrive qu'un ancien allié entre en guerre avec le protecteur, l'état protégé sera obligé de se déclarer pour ce dernier, auquel il est lié par des noeuds plus étroits, et par un traité qui déroge à tous les autres en cas de collision.
items.sourcePassage: Si Gentium foederatarum una sese in tutelam dat Genti cuidam tertiae; foedus subsistit.

items.question: What is an unauthorized promisor (sponsor) bound to when the state disavows his promise?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 475 holds that a sponsor whose sponsio is not ratified owes the other party full indemnity (id quod interest), on the private-law ground that one who contracts without mandate answers for the loss. Vattel denies that private-law reasoning applies to a public agent promising acts of his sovereign. Absent an express undertaking or custom, the sponsor owes only a good-faith effort to obtain ratification, and indemnity is presumed only where its matter lies within his power.
items.passage: tout ce à quoi il semble que sa parole l'oblige, c'est de faire de bonne foi tout ce qu'il peut faire légitimement, pour engager le souverain à ratifier ce qu'il a promis
items.sourcePassage: Si sponsio non fuerit ratihabita ; sponsor ei, cui spospondit, tenetur ad id, quod interest.

items.question: Are the sovereign's and the state's debts binding on the nation, and within what limits?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 479 holds that debts the ruler contracts with private persons for the cause of the republic bind successors and people, with the agreed interest. Vattel accepts the rule but limits it. Ruinous debts contracted without necessity do not bind the nation, and a sovereign without the power to tax has no power to create national debts.
items.passage: le conducteur, le souverain à qui elle n'a point confié le droit de lui imposer des taxes, des contributions, de faire, en un mot, de son autorité des levées de deniers, n'a point non plus le droit de l'obliger par ses emprunts, de créer des dettes à l'état
items.sourcePassage: si Rector civitatis aes alienum, a privatis Reip. causa suscipit, successores quoque et populus ad id luendum et usuras, utpote in se non illicitas (§. 1406. part. 4. Jur. nat.), conventas solvendum tenentur

items.question: What are pledges, engagements, hypothecs and antichresis between nations?
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 1150 holds that when a whole province or part of the territory is handed over as security, an antichretic pact is joined to the pledge. Vattel treats the delivery of a town or province as an engagement and calls the pact antichresis only when the revenues are ceded in place of the interest. For Vattel the right to the revenues requires a separate cession and does not follow from the delivery itself.
items.passage: et si on lui en cede les revenus, en équivalant de l'intérêt de la dette, c'est le pacte qu'on appelle d'antichrese.
items.sourcePassage: Enimvero si integra provincia, aut certa territorii pars in securitatem crediti, vel quacunque de causa debiti traditur; pactum antichresticum ad oppignorationem accedit.

items.question: What are pledges, engagements, hypothecs and antichresis between nations?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 485 holds that a province or part of the territory handed over as security carries an antichretic pact by that fact, since the only purpose of delivery beyond a hypothec and a garrison is to draw the revenues in lieu of interest. Vattel holds that the creditor who receives the place holds it by title of engagement, and that antichresis exists only if the revenues are ceded to him as the equivalent of interest. Wolff infers the cession of revenues from the delivery. Vattel requires it to be agreed.
items.passage: et si on lui en cede les revenus, en équivalant de l'intérêt de la dette, c'est le pacte qu'on appelle d'antichrese.
items.sourcePassage: Si integra provincia, aut certa territorii pars in securitatem pecuniae creditae, vel alia quacunque de causa debitae traditur; pactum antichresticum ad oppignorationem accedit.

items.question: What is pledged in a hostage, and what may be done to him if the giver defaults?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 532 holds that if the giver defaults the hostage either becomes a slave or is held as a captive, but may not be killed. Vattel holds that only the liberty of hostages is pledged and that on default they may be kept in captivity. Vattel drops reduction to slavery and gives captivity as the only consequence.
items.passage: La liberté seule des otages est engagée ; et si celui qui les a donnés manque à sa parole , on peut les retenir en captivité.
items.sourcePassage: obses vel fit servus, vel tanquam captivus retinetur, interfici autem nequit.

items.question: May a hostage be retained for his own acts or debts incurred while a hostage?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 505 holds that a hostage may be retained as a debtor until the costs of his maintenance are repaid and the debts he contracted are paid. Vattel holds that a hostage may be retained for his own acts, including offences committed against the nation that keeps him, as well as for debts contracted in the country. Vattel extends the ground of retention from contractual debt to delict.
items.passage: Mais on peut retenir un otage pour ses propres faits , pour des attentats commis, ou pour des dettes contractées dans le pays, pendant qu'il est en otage.
items.sourcePassage: quamdiu impensae in alimenta factae non fuerint restitutae, nec debita, quae obses contraxit, soluta, obses retineri potest ut debitor.

items.question: What happens to a hostage who succeeds to the crown
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 519 holds that a hostage who succeeds to the giver's throne is freed once another suitable person is put in his place, since the receiver never acquired a right to hold the king. Vattel holds the same release on substitution of an equivalent security, but only where the giving state has kept the treaty. If that state has broken its word, Vattel allows the receiver to take advantage of the succession and keep the more valuable hostage.
items.passage: En cas que cet état eut manqué à sa parole , on profiteroit avec raison d'un événement qui lui rendroit l'otage beaucoup plus précieux , et sa délivrance plus nécessaire.
items.sourcePassage: alio idoneo in locum sui substituto ipse liberatur.

items.question: What is the fate of the hostage when the giver breaks faith
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 532 holds that when the giver breaks faith the hostage either becomes a slave or is held as a captive. Vattel holds that the hostage becomes a prisoner who may be kept in perpetual captivity, and adds that, being released from all obligation to the sovereign who abandoned him, he may give himself as a subject to his keeper or be freed on agreed terms. Vattel omits slavery and dissolves the hostage's bond to his own sovereign.
items.passage: Et comme l'otage n'est plus tenu à rien envers le souverain, qui l'a abandonné par une perfidie , s'il veut se donner à celui qui est devenu le maître de sa destinée , celui - ci pourra acquérir un sujet utile , au lieu d'un prisonnier misérable , objet importun de sa commisération.
items.sourcePassage: obses vel fit servus, vel tanquam captivus retinetur, interfici autem nequit.

items.question: Examples: whether 'allies' in a treaty includes future allies; the liberty promised to Carthage
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 670 holds that allies named in a treaty are only those allied at the time, not future allies, unless the treaty says so expressly, because interpretation follows what the parties probably had in mind. Vattel holds that a clause binding each party not to harm the other's allies is favourable and must be extended to all present and future allies. Vattel decides the scope of the word by the favourable or odious character of the clause, not by the parties' probable thought at the time of contracting.
items.passage: et sur ce pied-là , il est si favorable à tous égards , si conforme à l'humanité et aux sentimens qui doivent unir deux alliés qu'on doit sans difficulté l'étendre à tous les alliés présens et à venir.
items.sourcePassage: socii tantum intelliguntur, qui nunc sunt, non vero futuri, nisi expresse dicatur, et qui nunc sunt, et qui futuri sunt.

items.question: Rule 9: whether a sworn treaty prevails over an unsworn one in a collision
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 427 holds that an oath induces no obligation beyond the one arising from the treaty, so swearing gives a treaty no right of precedence. Vattel holds that the oath adds new force to the obligation, so that a sworn treaty prevails over an unsworn one when other things are equal. Both keep the priority of the earlier ally, but Vattel makes the oath a ground of preference that Wolff denies.
items.passage: parce que le serment ajoute une nouvelle force à l'obligation
items.sourcePassage: Juramentum enim non aliam inducit obligationem, quam quae ex foedere oritur

items.question: How freely a nation or its ruler may waive rights and grievances
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 568 holds that every nation may waive its grievances and dispose of its right as it sees fit or as prudence advises. Vattel holds that the sovereign is only the administrator of the nation's rights and may dispose of them only as the nation would presumably do. Vattel adds a limit on the ruler's discretion that Wolff's rule for the nation does not contain.
items.passage: Les droits de la nation sont des biens dont le souverain n'est que l'administrateur ; il ne doit en disposer que comme il a lieu de présumer que la nation en disposeroit elle - même.
items.sourcePassage: Unamquamque Gentem de jure suo disponere posse, prouti sibi visum fuerit, vel prudentia suadet

items.question: Whether and when parties are bound by an arbitral award
items.comment: Wolff, Institutiones § 770 holds that the parties to a compromise are bound to acquiesce in the arbiter's award. Vattel holds that a manifestly unjust award, or one exceeding the matter submitted, does not bind the parties. The exception for manifest injustice and excess of mandate is absent from Wolff's rule.
items.passage: si par une sentence manifestement injuste et contraire à la raison, les arbitres s'étoient eux-mêmes dépouillés de leur qualité, leur jugement ne mériteroit aucune attention
items.sourcePassage: Partes igitur litigantes in laudo acquiescere tenentur

items.question: May a nation take arms without first trying conciliation
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 574 holds that under the voluntary law of nations arms may be taken without first trying conference or compromise, and that each nation's own judgment on the matter must stand. Vattel admits the same permission but requires the sovereign to be able to justify before the world that the offers of peace are a ruse. He denies that a nation's mere suspicions suffice, where Wolff leaves the judgment to each nation.
items.passage: Prétendre s'autoriser de ses seuls soupçons, c'est ébranler tous les fondemens de la sûreté des nations.
items.sourcePassage: standum sit uniuscujusque de istis judicio

items.question: Which goods may be seized in reprisals
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 495 holds that the goods of citizens are naturally bound for the debts of their nation, without exception. Vattel draws the same rule for reprisals but exempts a deposit entrusted to the public faith, such as foreign money placed in the public funds.
items.passage: pourvû que ce ne soit pas un dépôt confié à la foi publique
items.sourcePassage: Bona civium seu subditorum obligata sunt naturaliter pro debitis civitatis, seu Gentis.

items.question: Who indemnifies the subject whose goods are taken in reprisals
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 598 holds that those who gave cause to reprisals must indemnify the fellow citizens who suffer by them, since within the state one citizen's act cannot be imputed to another. Vattel holds that the sovereign must indemnify the subject on whom reprisals fall, because the loss is a debt of the state of which each citizen bears only his share. The two assign the duty of compensation to different parties on different grounds.
items.passage: c'est alors au souverain à dédommager celui de ses sujets sur qui sont tombées les représailles ; c'est une dette de l'état ou de la nation, dont chaque citoyen ne doit supporter que sa quote-part.
items.sourcePassage: Qui causam dederunt repressaliis, damna iis resarcire debent, quibus eam ob causam aliquid decedit.

items.question: What counts as a refusal of justice justifying reprisals
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 587 holds that the civil-law presumption of a confirmed sentence's justice does not hold between nations, so that a foreign sentence is not taken as just whether well or badly given. Vattel holds that the law of nations requires reciprocal regard for foreign jurisdiction for the same reason as the civil-law presumption, and obliges subjects to submit to foreign sentences in all doubtful cases. Both treat a manifestly unjust sentence as a denial of justice, but Vattel extends to nations the presumption that Wolff rejects.
items.passage: Le droit des gens prescrit aux nations ces égards réciproques pour la jurisdiction de chacune, par la même raison que la loi civile ordonne dans l'état, de tenir pour juste toute sentence définitive renduedans les formes.
items.sourcePassage: inter Gentes sententia judicis seu bene, seu male prolata pro vera et justa non habetur, etiamsi a superiore fuerit confirmata.

items.question: Must reprisals be preferred to war, and when is war rather than reprisal required?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 606 holds that war may not be declared while reprisals can repair the injury or obtain satisfaction, and that war becomes just when reprisals cannot. Vattel keeps the preference for reprisals but holds that in a dispute over a contested right, as opposed to a wrong received, reprisals are condemnable and a declaration of war must follow. Wolff draws no such distinction between kinds of dispute.
items.passage: Lorsqu'il s'agit dans le différend, non d'une voie de fait, d'un tort reçu, mais d'un droit contesté ; après que l'on a inutilement tenté les voies de conciliation, ou les moyens pacifiques d'obtenir justice, c'est la déclaration de guerre qui doit suivre, et non de prétendues représailles
items.sourcePassage: quamdiu autem per illas injuria reparari, aut ob irreparabilem satisfactio obtineri potest, bellum parti adversae indicere naturaliter non licet

items.question: Is every citizen obliged to bear arms for the state?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 749 holds that all subjects able to serve are bound to military service only in a case of extreme necessity, and that outside that case those useful to the state in other callings are not bound and are not to be conscripted. Vattel holds that every citizen able to bear arms must take them at the first command of the holder of the war power. Vattel makes the obligation itself unconditional and leaves the sparing of useful citizens to the prudence of government (III.10), where Wolff limits the obligation itself.
items.passage: Quiconque est en état de porter les armes , doit les prendre , au premier commandement de celui qui a le pouvoir de faire la guerre.
items.sourcePassage: ita nec omnes promiscue ad operas militares praestandas obligantur, nisi extrema adfuerit necessitas

items.question: Whom may the sovereign enrol, and by what means?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 749 holds that outside extreme necessity those able to render other useful services and to contribute to war costs are not to be conscripted, and that a levy contrary to this is an abuse of the right of conscription. Vattel holds that the sovereign may enrol whomever he pleases in time of need, and only advises him to choose fit men and, where possible, volunteers. Wolff's restriction is a limit of right, Vattel's preference for volunteers is a counsel of propriety.
items.passage: Puisque tout citoyen ou sujet est obligé de servir l'état , le souverain est en droit d'enrôler qui il lui plaît , dans le besoin.
items.sourcePassage: extra hunc casum milites conscribendi non sunt, qui alias Reip. utiles ac necessarias operas praestare et ad sumtus bellicos contribuere possunt

items.question: Who is exempt from bearing arms (women, clergy, magistrates)?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 752 holds that nature does not bar women from military service, since experience shows they are not unfit for it by reason of sex. Vattel exempts women as a class, on the ground that rules must follow what is ordinary, that women are needed for other tasks, and that mixing the sexes in armies is inconvenient. Both deny the clergy any natural exemption; they differ on women.
items.passage: Par cette raison , on exempte les vieillards , les enfanset les femmes.
items.sourcePassage: Foeminas a bellorum ministerio non arcet natura, quas propter sexum ad id non esse ineptas, experientia comprobat

items.question: Liability of a subordinate who falsely claims power
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 774 holds that a subordinate power which claims a greater right than it has is liable to the deceived party both for the damage and to punishment, and may also be punished by its sovereign. Vattel holds the subordinate liable only to repair the damage, and assigns punishment to its own sovereign as a duty of justice. The deceived party's own right to punish drops out.
items.passage: elle est naturellement tenue du dommage causé par sa fraude , et obligée à le réparer.
items.sourcePassage: tenetur ei, cum quo actum est, non modo de damno per demonstrata n. 1. verum etiam ad poenam.

items.question: How can defence become just against an originally just offensive war?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 629 holds without exception that defensive war against a just offensive war is unjust, and requires the wrongdoer to offer equitable terms before open combat. Vattel holds that once just satisfaction has been offered and refused, the attacker's hostilities become unjust and the defender's arms just. Vattel makes the refused offer a condition that converts the justice of the war, where Wolff states the offer only as a duty.
items.passage: l'on oppose désormais de justes armes à ses hostilités, devenues injustes, parce qu'elles n'ont plus de fondement
items.sourcePassage: injustum vero est defensivum si offensivum fuerit justum

items.question: When a war is nonetheless held legitimate on both sides (good faith, doubtful cause, invincible error)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 634 holds that only one side's arms are just, that a party in good faith still does not act justly, and that in a doubtful cause the judgement on justice stays suspended even after victory. Vattel holds that in any doubtful cause the arms of both parties must pass as equally legitimate as to external effects until the cause is decided, on the ground of the equality and independence of nations. Vattel adds a rule of external legitimacy for both belligerents that Wolff's section does not admit.
items.passage: les armes des deux parties qui se font la guerre doivent passer également pour légitimes, au moins quant aux effets extérieurs, et jusqu'à ce que la cause soit décidée
items.sourcePassage: uterque bona quidem fide agit ; non tamen juste, cum juste agere nequeat nisi is, qui jure agit

items.question: Whether and how appearances of danger from a rising neighbour give a right to use force preventively
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 650 grants the right to break a growing power by arms only when that nation openly plans to subjugate others and has already done an injury, however slight. Vattel sets aside the requirement of an injury received and allows a nation to demand securities, and to strike if they are refused, once a neighbour about to gain formidable power has given signs of injustice or ambition. The point of difference is the injury: Wolff makes an actual injury the condition, Vattel makes a reasonable presumption of ill will, weighed against the magnitude of the danger, sufficient.
items.passage: Dès qu'un état a donné des marques d'injustice, d'avidité, d'orgueil, d'ambition, d'un desir impérieux de faire la loi, c'est un voisin suspect, dont on doit se garder : on peut le prendre au moment où il est sur le point de recevoir un accroissement formidable de puissance, lui demander des sûretés, et s'il hésite à les donner, prévenir ses desseins par la force des armes
items.sourcePassage: si qua Gens consilia manifesta agitet de aliis Gentibus sibi subjiciendis, levissima injuria jus dat vi armata potentiam crescentem labefactandi

items.question: Does the right to make war lapse when equitable terms are offered
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 711 holds that when equitable terms of peace are offered to the party declaring war, they must be accepted and war abstained from. Vattel holds the same but requires that the offers be accompanied by security, since one need not be put off by empty proposals. He adds that a sovereign's word is sufficient security unless he is known to be perfidious.
items.passage: Bien entendu que les offres doivent être accompagnées de sûreté ; car on n'est point obligé de se laisser amuser par de vaines propositions.
items.sourcePassage: Quodsi ergo aequae conditiones offerantur bellum denuncianti ; cessat belli gerendi ratio, consequenter eaedem acceptandae et a bello abstinendum.

items.question: May the declaration be omitted in an offensive war when the enemy admits no envoy?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 714 allows the declaration of an offensive war to be omitted only when the enemy admits no envoys, no letter can be sent and no third party can carry the declaration, the impossibility being the enemy's fault. Vattel holds that refusal to admit a minister or herald suffices, and that the declaration is then made by publication in one's own states or on the frontier. Vattel also excuses sending a herald where the enemy's treatment of envoys makes it dangerous.
items.passage: on peut , quelle que soit d'ailleurs la coutume , se contenter de la publier dans ses propres états , ou sur la frontiere
items.sourcePassage: Si is, cui bellum denunciandum, nec legatos admittit nec adsit occasio mittendi epistolam, nec denunciatio per tertium fieri possit; denunciatio belli offensivi omittenda.

items.question: What must the inhabitants do when a foreign army enters before war is declared?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 718 holds that inhabitants must not resist an army that enters to declare war and announces peaceful intent, because its entry is lawful and resistance injures it. Vattel holds the same but adds that such an army may be refused entry into fortified places and cannot demand it. He grounds the inhabitants' restraint in their lack of the sovereign's order and lets them occupy advantageous posts and defend them if attacked.
items.passage: Bien entendu qu'on ne lui permettra point l'entrée dans les places fortes , et qu'il ne peut la demander.
items.sourcePassage: isto casu et incolae vi se eidem opponere non debent, qui vero hoc facere audeat, in eos licita animadversio.

items.question: Why legitimate war differs from brigandage (grounds of the distinction)
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 778 holds that whoever wages an unjust war is a robber, invader and brigand, since all force in an unjust war is without right. Vattel reserves the name of brigandage for war undertaken without any right and without even an apparent cause. A war declared in form over a dispute has, by the voluntary law of nations, the same effects on both sides whatever the justice of the cause.
items.passage: Entreprise sans aucun droit , sans sujet même apparent , elle ne peut produire aucun effet légitime , ni donner aucun droit à celui qui en est l'auteur.
items.sourcePassage: Qui bellum injustum gerit praedo, invasor ac latro est.

items.question: Status of immovables held by foreigners in enemy country, and enemy subjects' immovables at home
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 842 holds that immovables held in enemy territory by any foreigner, neutral or not, are hostile things, because the land is subject to the territorial jurisdiction. Vattel accepts the rule on the same ground but adds that modern usage grants safeguards to houses and lands held by foreigners in enemy country. The added usage removes most of the practical effect of the classification.
items.passage: on donne des sauve - gardes aux maisons, aux terres que des étrangers possedent en pays ennemi
items.sourcePassage: Immo in genere bona immobilia in territorio hostili possessa a peregrino res hostiles sunt.

items.question: Are debts owed to the enemy by third parties enemy property that may be seized or confiscated?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 729 holds without qualification that whatever is owed to my enemy, even by a non-enemy debtor, counts among hostile things. Vattel accepts this in principle but exempts rights granted by a third party in which that party has an interest, such as rights of commerce. He also holds that general European usage now bars confiscating debts owed to the enemy, and that breaching this usage violates public faith.
items.passage: Et dès que cet usage est généralement reçu, celui qui y donneroit atteinte blesseroit la foi publique ; car les étrangers n'ont confié à ses sujets, que dans la ferme persuasion que l'usage général seroit observé.
items.sourcePassage: ea, quae debentur hosti meo, etiamsi debitor hostis non sit, in numero rerum hostilium sunt

items.question: Is there a tacit just-war clause in peacetime war alliances, and how far does it release the ally?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 659 holds that every war alliance made in peacetime carries the tacit clause "if the war is just". Vattel accepts the clause but confines it to an evidently unjust war and requires the bound ally to presume his partner's cause just in doubtful cases. Wolff applies a manifest-injustice test only later, in Jus gentium § 662, and states no presumption in the ally's favour.
items.passage: La restriction tacite ne doit s'entendre que d'une guerre évidemment injuste ; autrement, on ne manqueroit jamais de prétexte pour éluder les traités.
items.sourcePassage: id quod omni factum intelligitur sub tacita hac clausula, si bellum fuerit justum

items.question: When does the casus foederis arise under a guarantee of possessions, and how is it determined?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 662 holds that the casus foederis does not exist when the ally's arms are manifestly unjust, because of the tacit just-war clause. Vattel holds that under a guarantee of the ally's possessions the casus foederis arises on invasion, and that even against an attacker with a just cause the guarantor may refuse to let those possessions be taken while obliging the ally to give satisfaction. For guarantees the injustice of the ally's cause no longer cancels the obligation.
items.passage: Si quelqu'un les attaque pour une juste cause, il faut obliger l'allié à donner satisfaction, mais on est fondé à ne pas souffrir que ses possessions lui soient enlevées
items.sourcePassage: casus foederis non existit, si foederati manifesto injusta sunt arma

items.question: What is owed when allies of the same alliance fight each other, and what does 'allies reserved' cover?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 669 holds that when members of the same alliance fight each other the treaty binds the third member to neither and gives neither any right. Vattel agrees that no aid is owed but holds that the alliance still obliges the third member to offer good offices for a reconciliation. Failing that, he leaves it free to aid the party in the right.
items.passage: L'alliance ne l'oblige donc à autre chose qu'à interposer ses bons offices, pour reconcilier ses alliés
items.sourcePassage: In praesenti nimirum casu neutri sociorum ex foedere obligaris, atque neutri ex eo jus quoddam quaesitum

items.question: Does assisting my enemy make one my enemy, and who counts as his associates?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 730 holds that whoever associates with my enemy, by sending auxiliaries or subsidies or helping him in any way, is my enemy. Vattel cites this section and rejects the general rule as unsupported by principle and contrary to European usage. He holds that only those genuinely associated in the war count as enemies, so that supplying aid does not by itself make a state an enemy.
items.passage: Elle ne peut se soutenir par les principes, et l'usage de l'Europe s'y trouve heureusement contraire.
items.sourcePassage: Qui hosti meo se associat, veluti auxilia aut subsidia mittendo, aut quocunque modo eum in bello adjuvando; hostis meus est.

items.question: Are those who voluntarily aid my enemy without a treaty his associates (my enemies)?
items.comment: Wolff, Jus gentium § 730 holds that whoever aids my enemy in any way, by auxiliaries, subsidies or otherwise, is my enemy. Vattel holds that voluntary helpers are associates of the enemy, but that limited aid given by a nation which keeps friendly or neutral relations may be dissimulated, and that custom does not treat such aid, chiefly permission to levy volunteers, as an act of hostility.
